question: I have noticed that adults with greater abdominal obesity may have worse blood sugar control even at similar weight.
refined_question: Among noninstitutionalized US participants in NHANES 2017-March 2020 pre-pandemic (Age >=18 years; excluding pregnant at examination), is greater waist circumference (per 10 cm) associated with higher HbA1c, after adjustment for age, sex, race and ethnicity, income-to-poverty ratio, educational attainment, smoking status, and body mass index?
title: Association of Abdominal Obesity (Waist Circumference) With Glycemic Control (HbA1c) Among US Adults: NHANES 2017-March 2020 pre-pandemic
hypothesis: Greater waist circumference is associated with higher HbA1c independent of BMI.

pico.population: noninstitutionalized US participants in NHANES 2017-March 2020 pre-pandemic (Age >=18 years; excluding pregnant at examination)
pico.comparator: Lower levels of the exposure (per-unit contrast; quartile 1 in sensitivity analysis)
pico.covariates: Age, Sex, Race and ethnicity, Income-to-poverty ratio, Educational attainment, Smoking status, and Body mass index

covariate_notes.bmi: BMI adjustment isolates the contribution of central adiposity beyond overall weight ('at similar weight'). Expect collinearity with waist (VIF check).

model.rationale: Continuous outcome: survey-weighted linear regression (design-based Taylor-series SEs) estimates adjusted mean differences. A binary clinical threshold of the outcome is analysed as a sensitivity analysis.

adjustment_sets.label: Adjusted for age, sex, and race and ethnicity

missing_data.rationale: Complete-case primary analysis within the design; multiple imputation by chained equations as sensitivity analysis when covariates are missing.

sensitivity.label: Exposure in weighted quartiles (Q4 vs Q1, P for trend)
Alternative exposure: Abdominal obesity - waist >102 cm (men) / >88 cm (women)
Alternative exposure: Central adiposity - waist-to-height ratio >=0.5

rationale.statistician: Continuous outcome: survey-weighted linear regression (design-based Taylor-series SEs) estimates adjusted mean differences. A binary clinical threshold of the outcome is analysed as a sensitivity analysis.
rationale.epidemiologist: Covariates were selected as plausible common causes of waist circumference and HbA1c (minimal confounder set from the domain library): Age, Sex, Race and ethnicity, Income-to-poverty ratio, Educational attainment, Smoking status, and Body mass index. Body mass index: BMI adjustment isolates the contribution of central adiposity beyond overall weight ('at similar weight'). Expect collinearity with waist (VIF check). Variables on the causal pathway or sharing laboratory components with the outcome/exposure are excluded to avoid over-adjustment.

limitations: Cross-sectional design: temporality cannot be established and associations must not be interpreted causally.
Single measurement of laboratory values; within-person variability and chronicity cannot be assessed.
Residual confounding by unmeasured or imperfectly measured factors (e.g., diet, medications, menstrual blood loss).
Self-reported comorbidities and behaviours are subject to recall and social-desirability bias.
NHANES excludes institutionalized and active-duty military populations.

agent_notes.message: First clinical concept treated as exposure, second as outcome (swap in the UI if needed).
Diabetes (self-report, medication, or HbA1c >=6.5%): Diabetes status is defined partly by HbA1c and lies on the causal path; adjusting for it is over-adjustment.
Body mass index: BMI adjustment isolates the contribution of central adiposity beyond overall weight ('at similar weight'). Expect collinearity with waist (VIF check).

checks.title: Cross-sectional: temporality cannot be established
checks.detail: Results are reported as associations; causal language is blocked in the manuscript.

checks.title: Run the PubMed/MEDLINE novelty check
checks.detail: A stated hypothesis exists; checking prior NHANES work documents the a priori rationale and avoids re-running a crowded exposure-outcome pair.

checks.title: Approve to hash-lock the protocol before results
checks.detail: SHA-256 of the analysis plan is recorded at approval; any later edit voids the approval. All 8 prespecified sensitivity analyses are reported regardless of result; 5 subgroup/interaction tests are labelled exploratory.

checks.title: Add a named statistician or epidemiologist sign-off
checks.detail: Investigator approval is required to run; journals increasingly expect documented methodological co-authorship for large-database studies.

checks.title: Explicit, same-population comparator
checks.detail: Contrast: per 10 cm higher waist circumference; weighted quartiles (Q1 reference) as sensitivity. Both groups come from the same probability sample and eligibility criteria (no convenience controls).

checks.title: Outcome includes measured (exam or laboratory) data
checks.detail: Objective measurement captures undiagnosed cases, unlike code-based EHR outcomes.

checks.title: Prespecified adjustment set
checks.detail: Adjusted for 7 covariates. Mediators and definitional overlaps are removed automatically, and an E-value quantifies how strong unmeasured confounding would need to be.

checks.title: Executable methods with data provenance
checks.detail: Every result comes with the compiled plan, R code, reproduce.R and MD5 checksums of the exact CDC files - the methods section describes what actually ran.
checks.critique: Methods the platform cannot actually run

design_audit.framework: Criticisms of EHR-network (TriNetX-style) studies: comparator, outcome, temporality, confounding, rationale, prespecification, reproducibility, meaningfulness, oversight.

review.title: Waist and BMI are strongly correlated
review.detail: Adjusting for BMI isolates central adiposity but inflates variance; the engine reports VIFs.

review.title: Multiplicity
review.detail: Many subgroup/interaction tests - interpret as exploratory or adjust for multiple comparisons.
